passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Change to Nursery Hours

emails.subject: Session times from January — 12 weeks' notice
emails.body:
Dear Ms Ferreira,

We received the letter announcing that from 5 January the afternoon session ends at 3:30 rather than 4:30, with fees unchanged.

I want to be clear that I understand the reason given — you cannot recruit afternoon staff and I know from other parents that you have been trying since spring. I am not disputing that.

My difficulty is the notice. The letter is dated 28 October, which is ten weeks. Our contract specifies twelve weeks' notice of any change to session times. I mention this not to insist on the letter of the contract but because the two weeks are the difference between my being able to change my working pattern and not. My employer requires a month's notice for a change of hours and the request goes to a panel that meets monthly. Ten weeks means I miss the December panel and cannot change until February.

So my question is practical rather than legal. Can the change begin on 19 January instead of 5 January? That is twelve weeks from your letter and it costs you two weeks of a staffing problem you already have. If it cannot, I will manage, but I would like to know before I start rearranging things on the assumption that it cannot.

With thanks,
Sunniva Karlsen

emails.subject: RE: Session times from January — 12 weeks' notice
emails.body:
Dear Ms Karlsen,

Yes. The change begins on 19 January. You are right about the contract and right that two weeks costs us very little against a problem we have had since March.

I should tell you that you are the only parent who has raised the notice period, and that eleven families are affected. I have written to all of them today with the new date rather than only to you, because it would be indefensible to give you twelve weeks because you asked and give the others ten because they did not.

On the fee, which you did not raise. Charging the same for an hour less is not defensible and I am not going to attempt it. Afternoon fees reduce by twelve per cent from 19 January, which is the hour as a proportion of the session. I should have said that in the original letter and I did not, because I was focused on the staffing and not on what the letter looked like from your side.

One thing I cannot fix. If we recruit successfully in the spring I would like to restore the 4:30 finish, but I am not going to announce that as a plan when it depends on filling a post I have not filled in eight months. If it happens you will get twelve weeks' notice of it, which I imagine is the more useful commitment.

Regards,
Beatriz Ferreira
Nursery Manager

passages.title: What Childcare Costs Actually Decide
passages.content:
Debate about childcare costs is usually framed around affordability, and the number quoted is the fee. Research on how families actually respond suggests that the fee is only one of several constraints, and frequently not the binding one.

The clearest finding concerns hours rather than price. A place that does not cover the working day cannot support full-time work at any price, and part-time provision is disproportionately what is available. A parent offered a heavily subsidised morning session and no afternoon has been given something valuable that does not solve the problem they had. Programmes measured on places created can expand substantially without changing employment at all.

Predictability matters more than the debate acknowledges. Shift workers and those on variable hours cannot use provision that requires fixed weekly sessions booked in advance, which is what almost all formal childcare requires. The households least able to afford care are disproportionately those with least control over their schedule, so the eligibility and the usability point in opposite directions.

The second earner effect is where the arithmetic becomes visible. Because childcare costs are typically compared against one income rather than household income, the calculation is usually made against the lower earner's wage, and returning to work can produce a marginal gain small enough that the decision turns on transport costs or a single sick day. This is not a preference about work; it is arithmetic, and it resolves differently for the same person at different wage levels.

Informal care is the largest provider in most systems and is almost invisible in the statistics. Grandparents and relatives supply a very large share of hours, and that supply is contingent — it depends on proximity, health and the retirement age. Policy that assumes it will continue is relying on an input it does not fund, does not measure and cannot replace at short notice.

The implication is that provision should be judged on whether it lets a parent take a specific job, rather than on cost per place. A cheaper place at unusable hours is worse than a more expensive one that covers the working day, and the metric currently used cannot tell the difference.

passages.title: Should Childcare Be Free at the Point of Use?

viewpoints.name: Minister Fenella Achterberg
viewpoints.text: We expanded free hours and I would do it again, though the evaluation embarrassed us in one respect. Take-up was highest among households already using paid childcare, who substituted the free hours for hours they were buying — a real benefit to them and not the labour-market effect we funded it for. The families we most wanted to reach took up least, largely because the hours did not fit their work. I would fund it again and I would design the hours around shift patterns, which we simply did not think about.

viewpoints.name: Radoslav Petrov, nursery owner
viewpoints.text: I deliver the free entitlement and the rate does not cover my cost, so I recover the difference from paying parents and from charges for meals and trips. That is not a scandal, it is the only arithmetic available to me, but it means a policy described as free is partly funded by other parents at the same nursery. Set the rate at cost and I will stop. Until then, please do not describe what I provide as free without also describing who pays for it.

viewpoints.name: Dr Leonie Marchetti, economist
viewpoints.text: The employment effects of free childcare are real and consistently smaller than campaigners project, because the largest gains appear where care was previously unaffordable and much of the spending goes to families already working. That is an argument for targeting, and targeting has its own well-documented cost — means-tested schemes reach fewer eligible families than universal ones, because complexity is itself a barrier. I do not think there is a clean answer here, and I am suspicious of anyone who presents one.

viewpoints.name: Nadira Haddadi, parent
viewpoints.text: I qualified for free hours and could not use them. They ran 9 to 12, my shifts start at 6, and the nursery would not take my daughter earlier even if I paid, because staffing is set by the funded hours. So the entitlement existed, I was eligible, and it changed nothing about my life. When the take-up statistics counted me as not taking up my entitlement, that was accurate and it was not a choice. Somebody should ask why the boxes on that form do not include the reason.
